nameStory: The mudpuppy gets its charming name from an old folk belief that it barks like a puppy underwater! While this aquatic salamander doesn't actually make dog-like sounds, early settlers heard various water noises and blamed this mysterious, gilled creature lurking in the mud of lake bottoms.
description: The Common Mudpuppy is a permanently aquatic salamander that looks like it never quite grew up—it keeps its feathery external gills throughout its entire life. These rusty-brown salamanders have a stocky, lizard-like body with four stubby legs and can grow up to 13 inches long including their flattened tail. Unlike most salamanders that live on land as adults, mudpuppies spend their whole lives underwater in lakes, rivers, and ponds, breathing through those distinctive red gills that wave like tiny underwater ferns.

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Three pairs of bright red, feathery external gills that look like tiny underwater plants waving behind the head—no other New England salamander keeps external gills as an adult

idTips.label: Color/Pattern
idTips.description: Rusty brown to chocolate brown body with darker spots or blotches scattered across the back and sides, giving it a mottled appearance like wet tree bark

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Large and robust for a salamander, reaching up to 13 inches total length with a thick, muscular body that feels substantial and heavy when handled

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found completely underwater in permanent water bodies—never on land like other adult salamanders

idTips.label: Skin
idTips.description: Smooth, slimy skin that feels slippery and mucus-covered, helping it glide through muddy lake and river bottoms

habitat: Mudpuppies live in the deeper, permanent waters of New England's larger lakes, slow-moving rivers, and deep ponds, especially those with muddy or rocky bottoms where they can hide during the day. They prefer waters that stay cool year-round and have good oxygen levels to support their gill breathing. Look for them in Lake Champlain and other major water bodies, typically in areas at least 3-4 feet deep.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more active as waters warm, with breeding occurring in late spring when females lay clusters of eggs under rocks or logs in shallow areas.
seasonality.summer: Most active period for feeding and moving around, though still primarily nocturnal and hidden during bright daylight hours unless water is murky.
seasonality.fall: Continues normal activity as long as water temperatures remain moderate, building up energy reserves for winter.
seasonality.winter: Remains active under ice, moving more slowly in the cold water but still feeding and breathing normally through their gills.

funFact: Mudpuppies are like the Peter Pan of salamanders—they never grow up! They go through a process called paedomorphosis, keeping their juvenile gills and aquatic lifestyle forever instead of transforming into land-dwelling adults like most salamanders do.
confusionNotes: Mudpuppies are sometimes confused with large aquatic larvae of other salamanders, but remember: if it has external gills AND is longer than 4-5 inches, it's almost certainly a mudpuppy since other salamander larvae transform to adults before reaching that size.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name, mudpuppies are completely silent—they don't bark, chirp, or make any sounds at all. The 'puppy' name comes from old folklore and superstition, not from any actual vocalizations.
compareHints: The Common Mudpuppy is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique among local salamanders for retaining external gills as an adult. While hellbenders (not found in New England) are the only other large, permanently aquatic salamanders in eastern North America, they lack external gills and have flattened heads with loose, wrinkled skin folds instead of the mudpuppy's smooth skin and feathery gills.
